items.item: Monomorphization is why a generic call optimizes exactly as well as a hand-written non-generic one: by the time the optimizer runs, there is no generic code left at all, only one concrete body per type actually instantiated

at.step: One generic function, compiled once per concrete type

items.item: Counting monomorphized symbols only works unoptimized: at -O, LLVM's interprocedural constant propagation can fold a trivial single-call-site generic body away entirely, even with #[inline(never)], which blocks true inlining but not value-level folding, destroying the very symbols the proof needs to count

at.deep: Internals: what the proof actually shows

items.item: The cost monomorphization moves is real but asymmetric: it scales with the number of distinct concrete types instantiated against a generic function, not with how many times it's called, so a hot loop calling one type pays nothing extra for being generic

at.step: Zero run-time overhead is not zero cost

items.item: Outlining doesn't reduce the number of compiled copies, it reduces what's inside each one: the thin generic shim still gets duplicated per type, but the bulk of the logic moves into one ordinary function compiled exactly once and called by every shim

at.step: Pulling the loop out of the generic shrinks the duplicate

items.item: A naive generic function with its full body inlined into the generic boundary pays monomorphization's bloat cost in direct proportion to how much logic sits inside the generic wrapper, which is exactly the lever outlining pulls on

at.step: Skip the outlining: what happens to the duplicate?

items.item: impl Trait in argument position and a named generic bound compile to the same thing (an anonymous vs named type parameter); the difference that matters in practice is purely about whether two positions are allowed to diverge in concrete type, not about any run-time behavior

at.step: One shared bound instead of two impl Trait parameters

items.item: Return-position impl Trait is not generic at all despite the shared keyword: the function, not the caller, picks the concrete type, and it's fixed at compile time for that function — this is why it carries no monomorphization choice at the call site the way argument position does

at.step: impl Trait in return position: one hidden, committed type

items.item: Box<dyn Fn> existed before impl Trait in return position specifically to let a function return "some type implementing Fn" without naming it; impl Trait in return position replaced that need for the common case where the caller never needs dynamic dispatch, trading one heap allocation per call for none

at.step: Returning it unboxed costs nothing extra; boxing it allocates

items.item: The allocation difference is real and measurable with a global-allocator counter, not a claim taken on faith: an impl Trait return makes exactly as many allocations as a hand-written function returning that same closure type directly would, which is zero beyond whatever the closure's own captures need

at.deep: Internals: what the proof actually shows

items.item: Neither impl Trait position changes what the compiler can prove about aliasing or mutability (Chapter 2's rule); they only change which party, caller or callee, gets to pick the concrete type behind the trait's interface
